title: Using the Internet to Promote Health Behavior Change: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of the Impact of Theoretical Basis, Use of Behavior Change Techniques, and Mode of Delivery on Efficacy
extended_summary:
This paper examines which characteristics of Internet-based interventions are associated with stronger effects on health-related behavior change. The authors note that online interventions had already shown generally small and variable effects, but prior reviews had not systematically linked specific intervention features to effectiveness. The study therefore asks whether use of behavioral theory, inclusion of specific behavior change techniques, and mode of delivery help explain variation in outcomes.

To answer this question, the authors conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials published between 2000 and 2008. Studies were included when the main intervention components were delivered via the Internet, participants were randomly assigned to intervention versus control conditions, and a post-intervention health behavior measure was reported. Across 85 included studies with a total of 43,236 participants, the authors coded intervention characteristics using established frameworks for theory use and behavior change techniques, and a new coding scheme for delivery modes such as tailored feedback, advisor contact, peer interaction, email, telephone, and SMS.

The studies covered a wide range of populations and health behaviors, including physical activity, diet, alcohol consumption, and smoking. Participants were not limited to educational settings; most were general or targeted health populations, though some studies involved adolescents and university students. The interventions were primarily delivered online, sometimes supplemented with other communication channels such as text messaging or telephone support.

The meta-analysis found that Internet-based interventions had a small but statistically significant average effect on health behavior overall (d+ = 0.16, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.23). More extensive use of theory and a greater number of behavior change techniques were associated with larger effect sizes. Interventions based on the theory of planned behavior showed comparatively larger effects, and supplementary communication methods—especially SMS—were linked to stronger outcomes. The authors conclude that more intensive, theory-based online interventions using multiple behavior change techniques and delivery modes are more promising than simpler approaches, while also stressing that findings should be interpreted cautiously because of heterogeneity across studies.
quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a health-behavior systematic review/meta-analysis, not a K-12 education or literacy study, and it evaluates generic Internet-based behavior-change interventions rather than educational AI/GenAI interventions relevant to the target evidence base.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects concern adult health-related behavior outcomes, so the paper provides no direct evidence on K-12 generative AI effects on reading, literacy, reading motivation, or related educational outcomes.
